title: Casino Side Bets in Canada: What They Really Cost
excerpt: Casino side bets promise huge payouts on blackjack and baccarat tables, but the house edge is brutal. Here is what each popular side bet actually costs Canadian players.
author: David Andersen
bodyHtml:
Sit down at almost any online blackjack or baccarat table in Canada and the felt will be covered in small circles that have nothing to do with the main game. Perfect Pairs. 21+3. Lucky Ladies. Dragon Bonus. Bet Behind. These are casino side bets, and they exist for one reason: the base games they are attached to are among the cheapest bets in the building, and the operator would very much like you to make an expensive one instead.

That is not a conspiracy, it is arithmetic. A well-played blackjack hand gives the house well under one per cent. A side bet on the same hand can give the house five, seven, or in some cases more than fifteen per cent. Understanding casino side bets is really about understanding how much you are paying for the thrill of a rare big payout, and deciding whether that price is one you are happy to pay.

Why side bets exist at all

Blackjack's low house edge is a marketing cost. Casinos accept it because the game draws players, and because most players do not use correct basic strategy anyway. But a table full of disciplined blackjack players is a table generating very little revenue per hour. Side bets solve that. They are optional, they are cheap to place, they resolve instantly, and they carry margins closer to a slot machine than a table game.

Online, the incentive is even stronger. A live dealer studio costs real money to run — dealers, cameras, streaming infrastructure, floor supervisors. Side bets are how those tables pay for themselves. If you have read our look at blackjack strategy for Canadian players, the contrast is stark: everything that guide teaches you to grind the edge down to a fraction of a per cent can be undone by one habitual side bet placed every hand.

The blackjack side bets you will meet

Perfect Pairs

You win if your first two cards form a pair, with escalating payouts for mixed pairs, coloured pairs and perfect (identical suit) pairs. Typical payouts are 5:1, 10:1 and 25:1 or 30:1. The house edge depends heavily on the number of decks and the exact paytable, but on a standard six or eight deck shoe it usually lands somewhere in the four to six per cent range. That is roughly ten times the cost of the hand you are actually playing.

21+3

Your two cards plus the dealer's upcard are treated as a three-card poker hand. Flush, straight, three of a kind, straight flush. Paytables vary enormously between providers, which is the important point — the same bet name can carry a three per cent edge at one studio and an eight per cent edge at another. Two operators offering '21+3' are not offering the same product, and the paytable is disclosed in the game rules if you look.

Lucky Ladies and its cousins

Pays when your first two cards total twenty, with bonuses for matched twenties and a jackpot for a pair of queens of hearts against a dealer blackjack. The headline payout is spectacular. The house edge is frequently in double digits. This is a lottery ticket wearing a blackjack costume.

Insurance

The most consequential side bet of all, and the one players rarely recognise as one. When the dealer shows an ace you are offered insurance at 2:1. Unless you are counting cards — which is not viable against the continuously shuffled or frequently reshuffled shoes used online — insurance is a losing proposition on every hand, every time. Declining it is not caution, it is correct play.

Baccarat and other table extras

Baccarat's banker bet is one of the finest bets in any casino, costing about 1.06 per cent after commission. The side bets bolted onto it are the opposite. The Tie bet, depending on whether it pays 8:1 or 9:1, costs somewhere between roughly 4.8 and 14.4 per cent. Player Pair and Banker Pair land around 10 to 11 per cent. Dragon Bonus and Perfect Pair variants sit in similar territory.

The pattern repeats everywhere. Roulette's basket bet on a double-zero wheel, the Any 7 in craps, the various bonus wagers on three card poker and Casino Hold'em — the mechanism differs but the trade is identical. You are exchanging a small, frequent, low-margin edge for a large, rare, high-margin one. Our guides to roulette and the wider casino games section break down the base-game maths for each of these in more detail.

How to think about them without being preachy

There is a version of this article that simply says 'never place a side bet' and stops. That is mathematically correct and practically useless, because people do not play casino games purely to minimise expected loss — if they did, they would not play at all. The more useful framing is cost per hour.

  • Know the paytable before you bet. Every reputable studio publishes it in the game rules. A 21+3 paying 100:1 on a suited three of a kind is a materially different bet from one paying 30:1.
  • Size side bets far smaller than your main bet. A $25 hand with a $1 side bet costs you pennies in extra edge. A $25 hand with a $25 side bet roughly triples your hourly loss rate.
  • Treat them as entertainment spend, not strategy. No side bet has ever been the mathematically correct play in a shoe game online. Placing one is a choice to buy variance.
  • Avoid stacking multiple side bets per hand. Three side bets at five per cent each is not a diversified position, it is one expensive position.
  • Never let a bonus wagering requirement push you into them. Some promotions exclude side bets from contribution entirely, meaning you pay the extra edge and get no credit for it.

The honest bottom line for Canadian players

Side bets are not rigged, they are not hidden, and they are not scams. They are clearly priced products that happen to be priced badly for the player. The casino discloses the paytable, the maths is public, and the choice is entirely yours.

What makes them worth writing about is how quietly they change the character of a session. A player who thinks they are grinding low-edge blackjack while placing a Perfect Pairs bet on every hand is not playing low-edge blackjack at all — their real house edge might be four or five times what they believe it is. If you like the occasional shot at a 30:1 payout, keep the stake small, keep it occasional, and keep the arithmetic in view. If you are chasing a bonus rollover or trying to make a bankroll last, the side-bet circles are the first thing to leave empty.
